title: One Headphone Ear Switched Into German, Yet Listeners Heard Normal English
description:
Experimental Chronicle — Colin Cherry (1953): The 'Cocktail Party Problem' — Shadowing One Ear While Going Deaf to Language Flips in the Other, grounded in E. Colin Cherry (1953) (The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America). Empirical findings show that in *1953 (Journal of the Acoustical Society of America), Imperial College telecommunications engineer Colin Cherry posed a deceptively simple question that stumped telephone and radar engineers for decades: 'How do we recognize what one person is saying when others are speaking at the same time (the "cocktail party problem")?'***.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how cochlea, auditory cortex, Broca's area coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that in Experiment 1 (both voices mixed identically onto ONE single audio channel with zero spatial separation), asking volunteers to pull apart two overlapping passages spoken by the SAME person's voice was brutal — they had to replay it dozens of times piecing tiny cliché phrases together word by word.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- E. Colin Cherry (1953). Some Experiments on the Recognition of Speech, with One and with Two Ears. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America. https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1907229
- E. Colin Cherry, W. K. Taylor (1954). Some Further Experiments upon the Recognition of Speech, with One and with Two Ears. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America. https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1907373
- Davide Castelvecchi (2015). 3D-printed device helps computers solve cocktail-party problem. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature.2015.18173
